text: Five ways to put a cache between your application and your database, and each one changes what you're trading away. Read-through: the application only ever talks to the cache, and the cache itself loads from the database the moment there's a miss. Cache-aside: the application owns that loading logic instead, checking the cache first and reading from the database itself on a miss, this is the one most teams reach for by default. Write-through: every write goes to the cache first, then immediately through to the database, so the two can never quietly disagree. Write-around: writes go straight to the database, skipping the cache completely, and the cache only gets populated later when that data is actually read. Write-back: writes land in the cache instantly and get flushed to the database asynchronously, which makes writes very fast and makes data loss possible if the cache fails before that flush happens. None of these is the "correct" one. Each is a different answer to how stale you can tolerate your cache being, and how much data you can afford to lose if something crashes at the wrong moment. Which of these five is your default, and which one have you actually been burned by?

text: Java records make data modeling cleaner. But cleaner code does not automatically mean cheaper runtime behavior. One thing worth watching in record-heavy code is allocation rate. A record is still an object. It costs the same as an equivalent final class with the same fields. The issue isn't records. It's how many objects we create, and how often. If a hot path keeps creating new instances during mapping, filtering, aggregation, API transformations or event processing, the JVM ends up allocating a large number of short-lived objects. For example: Database Row ↓ Entity ↓ Record DTO ↓ Mapped Record ↓ Response Record Each transformation may create another object. Individually, that cost is small. The JVM is built for short-lived objects: allocation is a fast pointer bump, and a young GC mostly pays for the objects that survive. At high throughput, it still adds up: More short-lived objects ↓ Higher allocation rate ↓ More frequent young GCs ↓ Objects that live slightly too long get promoted to old gen This does not mean records are bad. It means immutability has a runtime cost when object creation becomes excessive. The JVM can remove some allocations through escape analysis and scalar replacement, but only when the code gets inlined and the object doesn't escape. Performance-sensitive code shouldn't assume every temporary object will disappear. For hot paths, I usually ask: 🔹 How many objects are created per request or event? 🔹 Are we repeatedly converting between nearly identical DTOs? 🔹 Are Streams creating intermediate objects or boxing primitives? (Stream<Integer> vs IntStream) 🔹 Is the allocation rate increasing GC frequency? 🔹 Can the same data flow use fewer transformations? Records are excellent for: ✅ Clear data contracts ✅ DTOs and API responses ✅ Events ✅ Immutable-style domain data But in a performance-sensitive path, the better question is not "Are records efficient?" It's "How many objects am I creating, and how often?" That's where profiling beats assumptions: JFR allocation profiling, async-profiler in alloc mode, or JMH with -prof gc. Clean code and efficient code are not opposites. But at scale, we need to understand the cost of the abstractions we choose. What's the biggest allocation surprise you've found while profiling?

text: Your safest parallel service calls might come from a try block, not a CompletableFuture chain. JEP 543, Structured Concurrency, is now proposed to become final in JDK 28, due in March 2027. After seven previews, from JDK 21 to JDK 27, no further changes are planned. That matters wherever one request fans out to several services. With ExecutorService and Future, if one call fails, the others keep running unless you cancel them yourself. The JEP calls this a thread leak. With StructuredTaskScope, you fork the calls inside a try block. If one fails, the scope cancels the rest, and no thread is left running when the block exits. The catch is that cancelled does not mean stopped. Cancellation is an interrupt, so a call that ignores interrupts keeps the scope open until it returns. A downstream service that already got the request may still complete it. I'd start with one endpoint that calls two or three services in parallel. I'd make one service fail and another hang, then check leftover threads, time to cancel, duplicate downstream work and the JSON thread dump. Only then would I set a scope timeout from the caller's deadline and delete the hand-written cancel code. A deadline only holds when every call under it responds to interrupts. Teams on JDK 25 can try it today as a preview, with small API differences. LTS-only teams will get it as final in JDK 29, due in September 2027. When one parallel service call fails, what cancels the others in your code today?

text: Cleaning a RAG corpus by deleting what looks bad is how you lose answers. Record a decision for every block instead, and leave the document intact. Most published cleaning recipes were built for training models on web crawls, where discarding a page is free because billions remain. A knowledge base has one copy of each answer. Four rules worth keeping: • Count the documents a block appears in, not its occurrences. A footer in all 19 articles is boilerplate. A safety paragraph repeated three times in one manual is not. • Never normalise digits away before hashing. "10 working days" and "14 working days" become one block, and the index keeps whichever it saw first. • A near-duplicate score measures shared wording, not agreement. Two paragraphs differing in one number can score about 0.95 and contradict each other, so compare the numbers first. • Presidio's default entity list includes dates and person names, which are often the answer. Pass an explicit list instead. What can wait, and what cannot: • Four of the five stages can wait, because a wrong call is undone by changing the decision and chunking again • Personal data cannot, because the leak reaches logs and caches a rebuild never touches Which hurts your index more: a footer filling the top results, or two paragraphs that quietly disagree on a number?
